text:
Both premises are shaky. Einstein didn't fail math. He was top of his class in it and had mastered calculus by about 15. The myth likely came from a grading-scale change at his Swiss school (6 became the top mark, reversed from an earlier scheme) and from his failing the non-science sections of the ETH entrance exam at 16. Using the story with your kid would teach something false, and a kid who later learns that may discount the rest of your message.

"Grades don't matter" is also too strong. They matter for some things (course placement, scholarships, college admission, some careers) and matter little for others (most adult work, creativity, character). A kid who hears "they don't matter" and then sees a grade block something they want will feel misled.

A more accurate and more useful message: grades measure how well you did on specific tasks at a specific time, not your worth or your ceiling. They're feedback, not a verdict. Look at what a bad grade says about what to fix, and keep effort and curiosity as the real goals.

If the concern is a kid who's anxious or discouraged about grades, real examples work better than the Einstein myth. Plenty of people struggled in school and did well later, such as Thomas Edison's teachers reportedly finding him inattentive (also somewhat embellished) or, more reliably documented, many scientists who describe early academic setbacks. Pick one you've verified, or use someone from your own life.
